title: Bhagavato
hookLine: two translation apps, two English lines, one Pali title
tomorrow: what makes someone worthy of joined palms?

cards: Paste one sentence into two translation apps and you often get two English lines, both a little right. The third word of the homage has had that happen for a long time. Bhagavato.
On a Theravada chant sheet it usually reads: to the Blessed One. Rhys Davids, translating the suttas into English, wrote the Blessed One. Other translators chose the Lord, or the Exalted One.
And underneath all of them sits an older argument, inside the tradition itself, about what the title even points to.

teach.b: First the grammar, because it's quick. The title is bhagava. The ending on bhagavato does what tassa's ending did: it carries the to.
To the Blessed One. Now the argument. Buddhaghosa's Path of Purification, the great Theravada handbook, explains the title several ways and keeps them all.
Two of them pull in different directions.

The first view hears bhaga, fortune, a share of good. The Blessed One is the fortunate one: the one whose long training ripened into something rich enough to give away. Its best case: it tells you why people bow.
He has something to share, and the homage is thanks.

The second view hears bhagga, broken. The Blessed One is the one who broke greed, hatred and delusion. Its best case: it puts the weight on what he did, and a breaking is something others can train toward too.
Fortune names what he holds; broken names what he let go.

The handbook doesn't crown either one. It lists them side by side, and the chant carries both in a single word. So when you say bhagavato, you can hear the bow of thanks, or the sound of something snapping, or both.
That's the Blessed One: a title wide enough for an argument.

how: Theravada chant books usually render bhagavato as 'to the Blessed One'; teachers sometimes unpack the title with the readings Buddhaghosa gives in the Path of Purification.

s: bhagavato has one correct English translation
English translators have written the Blessed One, the Lord and the Exalted One; the Pali holds more than any one of them.
one of his readings: the one who broke greed, hatred and delusion.
the commentary picks one reading and rules out the rest

games.q: your friend reads bhagavato as 'the one who broke greed.' you prefer 'the fortunate one.' what's the strongest case for your friend's side?
o: it honors what he did, a breaking others can train toward too.
it's the oldest meaning, so it must be the only correct one.
it shows he was born unbreakable, so no training was needed.
games.why: the 'broken' reading puts the weight on what he let go, which others can practice. the fortune reading has its own best case: it explains the bow of thanks. the handbook keeps both.

practice: Let your eyes rest on one thing you honor: a photo of someone who taught you, a Buddha image if you keep one, a plant someone gave you.
Softly say namo tassa bhagavato, feeling the breath in the bh, then keep looking at it until the words have settled.

wordCard.voice: Bhagavato. To the Blessed One: the fortunate one, or the one who broke greed, hatred and delusion. The handbook keeps both readings. Word five of a little Pali.
